metadata.note: The Sacramento Northern Railway and its predecessors: the Northern Electric Railway (Chico – Sacramento, the 'North End', third rail) and the Oakland and Antioch / Oakland, Antioch and Eastern / San Francisco–Sacramento Railroad (Oakland – Sacramento, the 'South End', catenary), merged under Western Pacific control into the Sacramento Northern Railway on 1 January 1929. At 183 mi San Francisco – Chico it was among the longest interurban routes in North America, crossing Suisun Bay by train ferry. Passenger service only (Rule 1): Sacramento – West Pittsburg ended 26 August 1940, Chico – Sacramento and the North End branches 31 October 1940, the South End Bay Area locals 30 June / 1 July 1941, and the Chico streetcars 15 December 1947. Freight ran on parts of the system until the SN was absorbed into Union Pacific in 1983 and is not drawn. Horsecar operation (the Chico and Marysville horse railways the Chico Electric Railway rebuilt) is not drawn (Rule 5).
metadata.colour_note: Colours were pre-assigned by the coordinator: Northern Electric #5C4D9E, Oakland, Antioch and Eastern / San Francisco–Sacramento #3C8DBC, Sacramento Northern #2E5EAA. JUDGMENTS: (1) the Sacramento Northern Railroad (1918–1925) and the Sacramento Northern Railway (1925–1983) are treated as one company — the same name, the same trains, a WP-ordered corporate transfer — and share #2E5EAA. (2) Western Pacific bought control of the SN Railroad in 1922 and of the SF–Sacramento in 1927, but both kept running their trains under their own names until the 1929 merger and the SN thereafter ran as a separate WP subsidiary, so no feature is coloured as Western Pacific. (3) The Oakland and Antioch Railway (1909–1913), the Oakland, Antioch and Eastern (1911–1920) and the San Francisco–Sacramento Railroad (1920–1929) are one corporate lineage — leased, then reorganised out of receivership — and share #3C8DBC; they are split into separate features by name so each label says who ran the trains, but the colour does not change. (4) Lines owned by dummy or nominally independent companies but operated by the NERY or OA&E (Sacramento & Woodland, Marysville & Colusa Branch, San Ramon Valley RR, Sacramento Valley Electric) take the operator's colour. Rule 4 splits: Northern Electric → Sacramento Northern at the 28 June 1918 sale; OA&E → SF–S at the 1920 reorganisation; SF–S → SN at the 1 January 1929 merger.
metadata.mode_note: All intercity lines are mode 'interurban' (Rule 7: electric lines linking separate communities). The Chico Esplanade streetcar and the Sacramento – Swanston suburban line, both inside one built-up area, are 'streetcar'. The Mallard – Chipps Island car-ferry crossing is drawn as a short straight leg inside the Pittsburg – Sacramento features because trains rode the ferry intact.

metadata.geometry_quality: Most of the system is real-traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=SN and OpenHistoricalMap SN ways. Labelled approximations: street-grid sections in Chico, Yuba City, Sacramento, Woodland and Oakland's Shafter Avenue; the whole Danville, Walwood and Swanston (modern SacRT) lines; straight lines for the Dixon branch (11.6 mi), the Saranap – Crest Avenue hill crossing (2.0 mi), Diablo (0.7 mi), Oroville's lost Feather River crossing (1.0 mi) and the Mallard – Chipps ferry (0.5 mi). Each feature's geometry_quality gives its traced length against the documented mileage. Every trace passed reversal and revisit checks.
branches_deliberately_omitted: Hamilton City Branch (Northern Electric, Chico – Hamilton City, 11.1 mi): opened to passengers 13 September 1907; crossed the Sacramento River on a seasonal pile trestle and pontoon span; last operation over the whole branch December 1913 (Railroad Commission Decision 18442, 1927). Passenger years are sourced (1907–1913) but no grade survives in OSM or OHM and its route out of Chico (west from the SP depot, later the Ninth Street line) was not located, so drawing it would be almost all ruled line. Left for a future pass.

Key System trackage west of 40th & Shafter (to the Key Mole 1913–1939, to the Transbay Terminal over the Bay Bridge 1939–1941): SN trains ran through over Key System tracks without intermediate stops. Not drawn here; it belongs with the Key System layer, which another session is building.
Marysville – Yuba City streetcars (replaced by buses 16 February 1942) and the SN's Sacramento city streetcar lines (sold to Sacramento City Lines in 1943): routes and start dates not found.

Vaca Valley line's Willotta leg; the 1930 Creed connection; the Holland, Clarksburg and Chico airport lines; the Shasta Southern (Hamilton City – Monroeville): freight-only or passenger status not established.

Dixon branch (Rio Vista Junction – Dixon) spur of 1913 mentioned by Wikipedia as 'abandoned after a year or two' is taken to be the same line as the Sacramento Valley Electric Dixon Branch; drawn once.
not_yet_sourced: Every headway and avg_speed_kmh is an estimate except where a segment note cites a count (Woodland 1939–40, Chico streetcar 15/30 min, the June 1939 and January 1941 main-line patterns). A 1920s or 1930s public timetable (Official Guide or SN folder) would settle them.
Bay Point – Walnut Creek opening: May 1911 (1917 county history) vs 1910 (Wikipedia/Hilton & Due). Walnut Creek – Lafayette opening year (1911 or 1912).
Sacramento opening of the OA&E: September 1913 (county history, East Bay Hills Project) vs 3 September 1914 (Wikipedia).
Danville branch end: 1924 (Hilton & Due, local histories) vs 1920 (Groff).
Swanston end: 1932 (Trimble via Wikipedia) vs 1933 (Groff's account of the subsidy withdrawal).
Walwood branch: end of passenger service unknown (last evidence September 1916; gone by 1920).
Oroville branch: exact junction, mileage and Oroville terminal location.

Exact Chico – Durham private right-of-way south of 20th Street, the Yuba City street route (Bridge Street) and the pre-1925 Sacramento routes to the 8th & J depot.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. No North End running time was checked. The fastest 1939 train took 5 h 43 min over the 183 mi Chico–San Francisco through route (Wikipedia, citing Hilton & Due), about 32 mph including street running, the Suisun Bay ferry and Key System trackage; open-country running on the third-rail North End was faster, so ~55 km/h (34 mph) is used.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 90.18 mi against a documented 93 mi Chico–Sacramento route (Wikipedia: 'original 93-mile route'). About 77.6 mi follows OpenStreetMap ways tagged old_railway_operator=SN (abandoned grade, the 'Sacramento Northern Bike Trail' and 'Sacramento Northern Railway' ways). APPROXIMATED, about 12.6 mi in all: (1) 4.7 mi from the Chico depot at 1st and Main south to the first surviving grade north of Durham is drawn on today's streets (Main Street, Park Avenue, Midway) — the cars did run down Main Street and Park Avenue, but the private right of way south of 20th Street is not mapped and Midway stands in for it; (2) 1.9 mi through Yuba City to the Feather River is drawn on Yuba City streets (the line ran in Bridge Street; the drawn path may be a block or two off), then crosses the river on the mapped rail bridge; (3) about 3.4 mi south of Marysville follows untagged OSM rail beside the SN grade; (4) about 2.6 mi in Sacramento — the American River crossing to D Street on untagged OSM rail, then the street route on D, 15th and I Streets to the Union Traction Depot at 11th–12th and I — is on today's street grid. The Sacramento end is drawn to the 1925 Union Traction Depot for all years; before 1925 trains used the Northern Electric's own depot at 8th and J Streets, a few blocks west, which is not drawn separately. Gridley station check: the drawn line passes 2.7 km west of downtown Gridley, consistent with the interurban running west of the Southern Pacific town; not independently verified.

segments.note: Northern Electric Railway main line, Chico – Durham – Live Oak – Yuba City – Marysville – East Nicolaus – Rio Linda – Sacramento, 600 V DC with uncovered third rail in open country and trolley wire on city streets. NERY's first interurban, Chico – Oroville, opened in 1906 (drawn as its own feature); the line was pushed south through Marysville to Sacramento, with full service beginning 1 September 1907. Express trains carried names such as the Bay Cities Limited and The Steamer Special, the latter connecting at Sacramento with river steamers to San Francisco; parlor car Bidwell entered express service in January 1915. The NERY went bankrupt in 1914 and was sold to the new Sacramento Northern Railroad on 28 June 1918, where this feature ends. Headway is an ESTIMATE, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1 September 1907 full-service date is from the Wikipedia article (citing the Sacramento Evening Bee, 2 September 1907); the 1906–07 construction sequence, express train names and the 28 June 1918 sale are from Garth Groff's brief history on wplives.org. Headway not sourced.

segments.note: Sacramento Northern Railroad (bought the Northern Electric 28 June 1918). Western Pacific took control in 1922; on 4 November 1925 the property passed to the Sacramento Northern Railway, the WP subsidiary formed to group WP's interurbans. Both companies ran the trains under the Sacramento Northern name, so this feature keeps the SN colour throughout (see metadata colour_note). From 1925 trains used the new Union Traction Depot at 11th–12th and I Streets in Sacramento. 'Elverta Scoots', suburban cars on this line between Sacramento and Elverta (11 mi), ran from 1924 until 1931 over the southern end of this same track. Headway is an ESTIMATE, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1918 sale, 1922 WP control, the 4 November 1925 transfer to the Sacramento Northern Railway and the 1925 Union Traction Depot are from Garth Groff's brief history (wplives.org); the Elverta Scoot dates (1924–1931) are from his 'Suburban Service from Sacramento' page. Headway not sourced.

segments.note: After the 1 January 1929 merger with the San Francisco–Sacramento Railroad, through trains ran Chico – Sacramento – Oakland – (from 15 January 1939) San Francisco over the Bay Bridge; dual-voltage ex-OA&E motors worked through, while the third-rail-only Niles cars stayed north of Sacramento. In June 1939 the through service was down to three weekday trains Chico – San Francisco (the Comet and Meteor names belong to these runs). The last passenger train between Chico and Sacramento ran on 31 October 1940. Freight continued for decades and is not drawn. The 180-minute headway is an ESTIMATE averaging the 1930s decline; the only counted figure is the June 1939 three-trains-a-day service.
sources: Segment-level: the 1 January 1929 merger, the 15 January 1939 Bay Bridge service and the 31 October 1940 last Chico–Sacramento train are from Garth Groff's brief history (wplives.org); the June 1939 three-train service and the end in late October 1940 are from the Wikipedia article (citing Hilton & Due and the Chico Enterprise, 31 October 1940).

Overhead wire on Sacramento and Woodland streets, third rail between. Headway is an ESTIMATE, not taken from a timetable.

Local Sacramento – Woodland service: as late as 1939 eight weekday round trips; cut to four round trips in March 1940 (Sunday service restored at three after protests); all passenger trains ended 31 October 1940. The branch stayed in freight service (today Sierra Northern) and is not drawn after 1940. The 180-minute headway reflects eight round trips over a ~16-hour day in 1939 and is an approximation.

segments.note: In 1931 the SN asked to abandon Chico local service; the Railroad Commission refused, but headway was cut from 15 to 30 minutes, 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., no Sunday service. The city required the streetcars to keep running after interurban service ended in 1940 as the price of letting freight use its streets; wartime gas rationing filled the cars. The Esplanade line still ended at Chico Vecino in 1942, when the city paid for a freight-only extension to the airport (not drawn). Last car 15 December 1947 — the last scheduled passenger service on the whole SN.

Freight over the hills continued until 28 February 1957 and is not drawn.

Drawn alignment is the passenger-era one as far as OSM/OHM distinguish it; the 1951–54 Lisbon trestle rebuild is freight-era.

segments.note: Line across the Delta from Chipps Island to West Sacramento and over the M Street bridge to Sacramento, opened September 1913 (regular service to Sacramento from 3 September 1913). Trains crossed Suisun Bay on a car ferry between Mallard (West Pittsburg) and Chipps: the wooden ferry Bridgit from 1913 until a fire in 1914, then the steel Ramon (Groff: completed 1915; Wikipedia: in service by the end of 1914). The planned high-level bridge was never built. SOURCE CONFLICT on the opening: Wikipedia says full Oakland – Sacramento service began 3 September 1914; the 1917 county history and the East Bay Hills Project both give September / 3 September 1913, consistent with Bridgit being in service in 1913. 1913 is drawn. Headway is an ESTIMATE, not taken from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: September 1913 opening from The History of Contra Costa County (1917) and the East Bay Hills Project; the conflicting 3 September 1914 date and the ferry history from the Wikipedia article; Bridgit/Ramon dates from Groff's brief history. Headway not sourced.
